story_text.value:
I use shared markdown files to collaborate with agents. Their biggest complaint was that, when content changed, they needed to either re-read the full file or write code to find the difference.

So I made mdt. It's light - one binary, one sqlite file - and lets your agent track the changes to a shared file, so that it only reads the diff.

Ping me if I can make it better.

title.value: Show HN: Mdt – save tokens reading changes to Markdown

story_text.value:
Information pollution affects all of us. When we are served a random mix of important news, half-truths and “For You” posts from strangers in the same feed, our ability to make sense of the world are diminished.

Over time, it wears us down.

Robin is an open source Twitter/X client for iOS and Android. It restores a clean, chronological set of posts (only from people you follow.) You can hide posts using keywords (e.g. noisy politicians' names.) It also lets you fact-check claims quickly by long-pressing on the post.

Our goal is simple – Lower the amount of distractions and the unwanted stress caused by hot takes and replies from random people we don’t know nor care about.

Launch post: https://evergreen-labs.org/blog/introducing-robin

iOS: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/robin-non-algorithmic-x/id6817...

Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.evergreenl...

Public Repo: https://github.com/billylo1/Robin

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

Instant Search is the first accurate local AI file search that uses the latest embedding models from Perplexity to find the exact file (and page) with the content you’re looking for with a 95% hit rate.

Search never worked properly, especially with local files. Now, you can find the right image, document, or Obsidian file in seconds. Looking for your driver’s license? Just type “driver’s license”. Looking for a particular note? Just explain the context.

Why not Finder/Spotlight?

Spotlight is just a keyword search. It doesn’t understand file content. Instant finds the exact file you’re describing in under a second.

Why not RAG?

Traditional RAG models give you a single embedding vector per entire body of text. That means either you have a vector that’s not detailed enough to give you an accurate semantic representation, or it’s too precise and doesn’t contain enough surrounding context. Instant circumvents these problems by relying on a bidirectional late-interaction embedding model that works flawlessly.

How much space does indexing need? An average library of content needs less than 1GB of disk space.

Check it out, share with friends, and let me know your feedback! It's free.

story_text.value:
Hi HN! I love Anki and I've been using it for 5–6 months pretty much consistently. It's a wonderful piece of software, but its obvious downside is its UI. I love beautiful things, and spending 30–40 minutes daily on something that doesn't bring me aesthetic joy is kinda urgh...

So I'm building Amgi (암기, means memorization in Korean), an open-source plain-text spaced repetition system with FSRS. I started building it only a week ago.

Flash cards are simply Markdown files with pretty elegant syntax, so you are not tied to any app. Just open your flashcards folder in your favorite editor and add/edit straightaway:

  Q: What does FSRS stand for?
  A: Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler

  C: The capital of [France] is [Paris|city].
Amgi has a dashboard where you can see your streak & some statistics on your reviews, and a browser where you can search using queries similar to Anki's (deck:Name, #tag, is:due, etc.). It also supports LaTeX, images, audio and code blocks (incl. making cloze cards inside of them). And it has a cute installer! (I hope)

It can already import from Anki, but it's still pretty early and the only Anki collection I've tested on is my own, so expect some rough edges. Mac-only for now!

My own collection is public too, it's the actual one I use daily: https://github.com/alisheryeginbay/flashcards

Would love feedback, especially on the card syntax :)

story_text.value:
Sixteen years ago, I wrote a Java program which tried to pick the ideal move in a puzzle game called Drop7. On each turn, the player only has seven choices for their next move, but there is also an element of chance which turns this simple game into a surprisingly difficult problem involving search, hidden information, long-term planning, and chance.

I renewed my investigation this weekend, into whether there is an autonomous strategy that averages more than one million points per game. An experienced human player can score a million points with long-term strategic thinking, but the best automated strategies I could come up with are currently averaging around 300k-400k points. One of the easiest ways to contribute to advancing this research is to compete on the global leaderboard and submit your human strategy - https://drop7.dev/compete.

This project has also been an enlightening experiment into using agents as research collaborators and evidence collectors.

Repository: https://github.com/keshavsaharia/drop7-bench

I’d especially appreciate feedback from people who are knowledgeable in game theory, stochastic planning, learned value functions, or heavy-tailed evaluation. How would you approach long-horizon action ranking here? I’d also love to hear whether the research makes sense to someone encountering the project for the first time.

title.value: Show HN: Searching for optimal strategies in a puzzle game with chance (Drop7)

Hi HN,

Experimenting with new Content Mappers feature in TypeScript 7.1 beta, and come up with one usefull idea:

Why don't we try to import C, C++, Rust files directly into TypeScript and call native functions without manually writing all the bindings?

Super simple and stupid implementation, but let's see how it goes.

Technically, something similar was already possible with Volar.js, but TypeScript 7.1 makes the integration much more straightforward.

I’ve been struggling with Mermaid in Markdown for a while. I appreciate the technical finesse of its rendering, but the diagrams are often unreadable. So we wrote an alternative that is optimized for MCP and LLMs while still looking good to humans. The LLM can position elements, and it stays Markdown-compatible. It’s MIT licensed, and I hope you can use it.

our rational: https://uberblick.ai/blog/2026/why-we-dropped-mermaid

Cheers
